## DI-0301 asks IT a question nobody expected to be hard

Your Quality Analyst (QA) is closing in on the end of **DI-0301**, her data-integrity
self-assessment. DED-0458 — module 1's BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software)
donor-eligibility record — is settled on every ALCOA (attributable, legible, contemporaneously
recorded, original or a true copy, accurate) letter except "accurate," still open. Fairview's
paper donor file is settled as its own record of record. LAB-07 has a documented, fixable gap on
its fitness-for-use evidence. Today she's asking a question that sounds almost too basic to be a
real finding: "If BECS went down tomorrow, could we actually get DED-0458 back?"

The systems administrator's answer is quick and confident: "Of course. We back it up every
night." She asks him to actually show her. What he shows her is a nightly automated snapshot job
— a routine that copies BECS's database state every night so IT can recover quickly if the server
crashes or someone accidentally overwrites something. It works well, and it's been reliable. Then
she asks the follow-up question that actually matters: how long does a given night's snapshot
stick around before something newer replaces it? The answer: 30 days, on a rolling basis. After
that, it's gone, automatically, by design.

She sits with that for a second, because something doesn't add up. DED-0458 is a donor-eligibility
determination — a BECS record this course has already established lives on a multi-year retention
clock, not a 30-day one. If the only "backup" of that record disappears after a month, what
happens to the retention requirement the other 11 years and 11 months?

**Second thread, smaller but just as real.** While she's in records territory, she pulls the full
list of donor records 606.160(b)(1) (21 CFR 606.160, paragraph (b)(1)) requires Lakeshore to keep
— selection, deferrals, adverse reactions, the donor's full donation history. A donor who's given
many times over many years has one donor record tracking all of it. She asks: when does *that*
record's retention clock run out? Nobody has a clean answer. No citations yet — just a snapshot
job that deletes itself on a schedule, and a donor file with an ambiguous expiration date.

## Why this rule exists — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure both threads are circling. A record that can't survive to the end of its own
required retention period doesn't just have a documentation gap — it has a hole where the proof
used to be. If DED-0458 needs to be producible for years, and the only backup copy of it quietly
expires after 30 days, then from roughly day 31 onward, if BECS's own live database were ever lost
or corrupted, that record simply wouldn't exist anymore. Not "hard to find." Gone. An inspector
asking for a five-year-old donor-eligibility record doesn't care that IT had excellent uptime in
the meantime — they care whether the record can be produced today.

You already run the discipline this needs, under names you use constantly in disaster-recovery
(DR) planning: **RPO (recovery point objective)** — how much data you can afford to lose, measured
in time, if something fails right now — and **RTO (recovery time objective)** — how fast you have
to be back up and running. A 30-day rotating snapshot is a perfectly sound RPO/RTO choice for
ordinary DR. It answers "if the server dies tonight, how much work do we lose, and how fast can we
restore it?" — and for that question, 30 days of rolling snapshots, cheap to store and fast to
restore from, is a reasonable, defensible engineering decision. Nothing about it is wrong *as DR*.

Here's where the regulated world demands more, and it's worth being precise about exactly what
changes. Ordinary DR backup answers "can we recover from an outage quickly." A CGMP (current good
manufacturing practice) backup under 21 CFR 211.68(b) answers a completely different question:
"can we reconstruct this record's full, exact, complete state at any point across its entire
multi-year retention period?" A system can be excellent at the first question and come nowhere
close to answering the second — and that's exactly the trap here, because both things get called
"backup," in the same sentence, by people who mean two different things by the word.

## The rule in plain English

Three separate ideas, and DI-0301's two threads map cleanly onto them.

**First: 606.160(d)'s own retention clock is a fact this curriculum already has, not new ground.**
It was taught in full in `reading-a-cfr-citation` — individual product records retained at least
10 years after processing or 6 months past the product's latest expiration date, whichever is
later, indefinitely if there's no expiration date at all. That's the floor DED-0458 sits on. This
module doesn't re-derive that math. It asks what has to be true for a record to actually *survive*
to the end of whatever clock applies to it.

**Second: "backup" is a specific regulatory term under 211.68(b), not a synonym for "we copy our
data somewhere."** FDA's 2018 guidance — **guidance tier**, FDA's current thinking, "should"
language, the same source this course has used since module 1 — defines exactly what 211.68(b)'s
"backup" means, and draws the line DI-0301's first thread just ran into: a true, secure copy
maintained *throughout the record's retention period*, versus a temporary recovery copy meant to
survive a crash for a little while. Only the first one satisfies 211.68(b). A 30-day rotating
snapshot, by its own design, is the second — useful, real, and not what the regulation is asking
for.

**Third: retention for a dynamic record means keeping it dynamic, not just keeping a value.**
Module 3 already built the static/dynamic distinction — static is fixed data, like a printout;
dynamic is a format that lets someone interact with the record, reprocess it, view it a different
way. Module 3 and module 4 already settled that DED-0458's live BECS record is dynamic, and that
LAB-07's dormant export mode would be too, if anyone ever used it. Retention for a dynamic record
isn't "export the current value and keep that number for 10 years." It's keeping the record's full
metadata and its interactive, queryable nature intact — and the reader or access tools needed to
use it — for the whole retention period. A flat value, however accurate, is a different, lesser
thing than the record it came from.

**Fourth, the open one: donor records don't obviously share 606.160(d)'s clock at all.**
606.160(d)'s own text ties its interval to "the blood or blood component" — a specific unit's own
processing date and expiration date. A donor record isn't about one unit. 606.160(b)(1) requires
Lakeshore to keep a donor's selection history, deferrals, adverse reactions, and — specifically —
"records to relate the donor with the unit number of each previous donation from that donor." A
donor who's given many times over many years has one cumulative record spanning units with
different processing dates and different expiration dates, stretched across years. Which one
starts the clock for the donor's own record — the first donation, the most recent, or does the
donor record have to outlive every single unit's own clock, one at a time? 606.160(d)'s text,
read carefully, doesn't actually answer that. That's not a gap in this lesson. It's a gap in the
regulation's own plain text, applied to a record type it wasn't obviously written with in mind —
and it's exactly why a retention policy has to be worked out and documented record-type by
record-type, not assumed from memorizing one number.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 211.68(b) | "Two-eleven point sixty-eight, paragraph b" | Regulation tier. Requires a backup file of data, exact and complete, secure from alteration, erasure, or loss. | What Lakeshore's nightly snapshot has to satisfy — and, as currently built, doesn't. |
| FDA 2018 Data Integrity Q&A, Question 1e | "Question one, part e" | Guidance tier. Defines "backup" under 211.68(b) as a true copy maintained securely throughout the retention period; says a temporary crash-recovery copy doesn't satisfy that requirement. | The exact distinction between IT's DR snapshot and a real regulatory backup. |
| FDA 2018 Data Integrity Q&A, Question 9 | "Question nine" | Guidance tier. Electronic copies can serve as true copies only if they preserve metadata and the static-or-dynamic nature of the original. | What retaining DED-0458 actually requires, beyond keeping its surface value. |
| 21 CFR 606.160(b)(1) | "Six-oh-six point one-sixty, paragraph b, sub-one" | Regulation tier. Lists the donor records Lakeshore must maintain, including the record relating a donor to every one of their past donations. | The records whose retention clock DI-0301's second thread can't cleanly resolve. |
| 21 CFR 606.160(d) (one line, not re-quoted) | "Six-oh-six point one-sixty, paragraph d" | Regulation tier. Already fully taught in `reading-a-cfr-citation` — individual product records, 10 years past processing or 6 months past expiration, whichever is later. | The product-record clock this module builds past, not around. |

## The actual text

Start with 211.68(b) itself, quoted in full from `sources/cfr/211.68.md` — the regulation this
course has cited before for a different reason (module 7's interface context in `csv-and-becs`),
and now the load-bearing text for retention and backup specifically:

> Appropriate controls shall be exercised over computer or related systems to assure that changes
> in master production and control records or other records are instituted only by authorized
> personnel. Input to and output from the computer or related system of formulas or other records
> or data shall be checked for accuracy. The degree and frequency of input/output verification
> shall be based on the complexity and reliability of the computer or related system. A backup
> file of data entered into the computer or related system shall be maintained except where
> certain data, such as calculations performed in connection with laboratory analysis, are
> eliminated by computerization or other automated processes. In such instances a written record
> of the program shall be maintained along with appropriate validation data. Hard copy or
> alternative systems, such as duplicates, tapes, or microfilm, designed to assure that backup data
> are exact and complete and that it is secure from alteration, inadvertent erasures, or loss shall
> be maintained.

Read "shall be maintained" as doing real work twice in that passage: a backup file shall exist,
and it shall be designed to stay exact, complete, and secure from alteration or loss. It doesn't
say for how long, in so many words — that's where FDA's guidance fills in the practical meaning,
quoted verbatim from `sources/fda-guidance/data-integrity-cgmp-qa-2018.md`, Question 1e:

> FDA uses the term backup in § 211.68(b) to refer to a true copy of the original record that is
> maintained securely throughout the record retention period (e.g., § 211.180). Backup data must
> be exact, complete, and secure from alteration, inadvertent erasures, or loss (§ 211.68(b)). The
> backup file should contain the data (which includes associated metadata) and should be in the
> original format or in a format compatible with the original format.

"Throughout the record retention period" is the phrase DI-0301's finding turns on. For DED-0458,
that period is 606.160(d)'s own years-long clock — not 30 days. The same answer then draws the
line this module's whole scenario sits on top of:

> Temporary backup copies (e.g., in case of a computer crash or other interruption) would not
> satisfy the requirement in § 211.68(b) to maintain a backup file of data.

That sentence names Lakeshore's nightly snapshot job almost exactly — "in case of a computer
crash" is precisely what the systems administrator described it for. FDA isn't saying that kind of
snapshot is worthless. It's saying it's a different thing from what 211.68(b) actually requires,
and calling it "the backup" in a validation or quality document would be a real misstatement, not
a harmless shorthand.

Now the electronic-copies answer, quoted in full from the same guidance, Question 9 — this is what
retention actually has to preserve, not just a value:

> Electronic copies can be used as true copies of paper or electronic records, provided the copies
> preserve the content and meaning of the original record, which includes all metadata required to
> reconstruct the CGMP activity and the static or dynamic nature of the original records.
>
> True copies of dynamic electronic records may be made and maintained in the format of the
> original records or in a format that allows for the content and meaning of the original records
> to be preserved if a suitable reader and copying equipment (e.g., software and hardware,
> including media readers) are readily available (§§ 211.180(d) and 212.110).

Two requirements stacked in that passage: the copy has to preserve metadata, and it has to
preserve whether the original was static or dynamic. A dynamic record copied as a flat value loses
the second requirement even if every number in it is correct — the same lesson module 4 applied to
LAB-07's dormant export mode, now stated as the general rule it always was.

Last, the donor-records list, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.160.md`, 606.160(b)(1):

> (b) Records shall be maintained that include, but are not limited to, the following when
> applicable:
>
> (1) Donor records:
>
> (i) Donor selection, including medical interview and examination and where applicable, informed
> consent.
>
> (ii) Permanent and temporary deferrals for health reasons including reason(s) for deferral.
>
> (iii) Donor adverse reaction complaints and reports, including results of all investigations and
> followup.
>
> (iv) Therapeutic bleedings, including signed requests from attending physicians, the donor's
> disease and disposition of units.
>
> (v) Immunization, including informed consent, identification of the antigen, dosage and route of
> administration.
>
> (vi) Blood collection, including identification of the phlebotomist.
>
> (vii) Records to relate the donor with the unit number of each previous donation from that
> donor.

Clause (vii) is the one DI-0301's second thread actually turns on. It requires a record that ties
one donor to *every* previous donation, by unit number — which means the record itself is
cumulative by design, growing across a donor's entire donating history, not scoped to any single
unit's own processing and expiration dates. 606.160(d)'s retention clock, remember — one line only,
already fully taught elsewhere — ties its interval to "the blood or blood component." A cumulative
donor record isn't one blood component. It's the record of many, collected over years. The text
doesn't say which of those many expiration dates it should attach to.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) assessor
wouldn't ask whether Lakeshore has a backup policy. They'd ask for proof the specific record they
want, from whenever in its retention period they ask for it, can actually be produced.

**For BECS records like DED-0458:** can Lakeshore produce this exact record from three years ago,
right now, in a form that preserves its metadata and its dynamic, queryable nature — not just a
value someone remembers was correct. A bad answer sounds like "we back up BECS every night." A
good answer names the actual retention mechanism — distinct from the DR snapshot — that's designed
to survive the full retention period, and shows it working.

**For the nightly snapshot specifically:** what does it actually promise, in writing? A bad answer
calls it "the backup" without qualification. A good answer names it for what it is — a 30-day
disaster-recovery mechanism — and points to a separate, documented control that satisfies
211.68(b)'s actual retention-period requirement.

**For donor records:** evidence that Lakeshore has actually decided, and written down, how long a
cumulative donor record is retained and why — not a shrug, and not an invented precise number
presented as if it were self-evidently correct. A good answer can show the documented reasoning,
even if the reasoning is conservative (e.g., retaining the whole donor record as long as any
donation it covers could still be within its own clock). A bad answer either has no policy at all,
or states a number with no citation behind it.

## Common traps

**"We have backups, so we're covered."** This is the trap DI-0301's whole first thread exists to
refute. "Backup" is being used to mean two different things at once: IT's 30-day disaster-recovery
snapshot, and the 211.68(b) backup FDA's guidance actually requires — a true copy maintained
securely throughout the entire retention period. Having the first doesn't mean Lakeshore has the
second. They can both be true, and they usually need to be — a good DR snapshot and a real
long-retention backup solve different problems and can coexist, but only one of them is what
211.68(b) is asking for, and calling the wrong one "the backup" in a quality document is the exact
misstatement an inspector is trained to catch.

**"606.160(d) tells you how long to keep every blood-center record."** Not quite. 606.160(d) sets
the clock for individual product records tied to a specific unit's own processing and expiration
dates. It doesn't, on its own text, resolve a cumulative donor record's retention the same clean
way — the donor record covers many units, collected over years, and 606.160(d)'s language was
written with one unit's clock in mind. Treating "606.160(d)" as a universal answer for every
record type is exactly the shortcut this module exists to stop you from taking.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask, by name, what Lakeshore's actual 211.68(b) backup mechanism is — separate from whatever
  disaster-recovery snapshot IT runs.** If the honest answer is "they're the same thing," that's
  the finding, not a reassurance.
- **Push back the moment someone calls a 30-day (or any short-window) rotating snapshot "the
  backup" in a validation or quality document.** Ask them to name what it's actually for (crash
  recovery) and what satisfies 211.68(b)'s own, much longer requirement instead.
- **For any dynamic BECS record, ask whether the retention mechanism keeps it queryable and
  reader-accessible, or only exports a flat value.** A correct number isn't the same thing as a
  preserved record, by FDA's own Question 9 standard.
- **Treat the donor-record retention-clock question as a real policy gap to close, not a crisis to
  panic over.** The fix isn't guessing a number — it's documenting, in Lakeshore's own
  document-control procedure, a reasoned retention interval for cumulative donor records, the same
  record-type-by-record-type discipline `document-control-and-records` already recommended and
  left for this course to fill in.
- **When RPO/RTO numbers come up in a DR conversation, ask the follow-up question DI-0301 asked:
  "does this also satisfy our regulatory retention requirement, or only our uptime goal?"** The two
  questions sound similar and have completely different right answers.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: The systems administrator says, "BECS is backed up every night, so we satisfy 211.68(b)." Is a nightly snapshot that gets deleted after 30 days enough?

No. FDA's 2018 guidance (Question 1e) is direct on this point: a backup under 211.68(b) is a true
copy "maintained securely throughout the record retention period," and "temporary backup copies
(e.g., in case of a computer crash or other interruption) would not satisfy the requirement in §
211.68(b) to maintain a backup file of data." A 30-day rotating snapshot is a sound disaster-
recovery (DR) control — it answers "can we recover quickly from a crash," a reasonable RPO
(recovery point objective)/RTO (recovery time objective) choice. It does not answer the separate
question 211.68(b) actually asks: can this record be reconstructed, exact and complete, at any
point across its entire multi-year retention period. Lakeshore needs a distinct, longer-lived
mechanism to satisfy that — the 30-day job can keep doing its own job alongside it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: A donor has given blood at Lakeshore many times over several years. 606.160(b)(1)(vii) requires a record relating that donor to every one of their past donations. Exactly how long must that cumulative donor record be retained?

This is a genuinely open question, and the honest answer is "it's not fully settled by the text of
606.160(d) alone — document the policy, don't guess a precise number." 606.160(d)'s own retention
interval is tied to "the blood or blood component" — a specific unit's own processing and
expiration dates. A cumulative donor record isn't about one unit; it covers many, collected over
years, so it isn't obvious which unit's clock the donor record's own retention should attach to:
the donor's first donation, their most recent one, or every one of them in turn. **This is not a
regulatory requirement with one clean, citable number** — it's exactly the kind of gap a
self-assessment should surface and route to Lakeshore's own document-control procedure to resolve
and write down, the same way `document-control-and-records` already flagged that working out
record-type-specific retention schedules was a level of detail it wasn't building out. DI-0301's
job here is to flag the question precisely, not invent a false-precise answer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: DED-0458 is settled as a dynamic, Part 11 record (module 3). Does retaining it for 606.160(d)'s full interval just mean keeping its data values intact for that whole period?

Not quite — and this is the central practical point of this module. FDA's 2018 guidance (Question
9) requires that a true copy of a record preserve "the static or dynamic nature of the original
records," along with "all metadata required to reconstruct the CGMP activity." For DED-0458, that
means retention has to keep the record's full metadata (who touched it, when, what changed) and
its interactive, queryable nature intact for the whole retention period — with a suitable reader or
access tool still available to use it — not just a flat exported value that happens to match what
the record said on the day it was created. A correct number, with no metadata and no way to
interact with it, is a different and lesser thing than the record 211.68(b) and Question 9 actually
require Lakeshore to retain.
:::

## Where this goes next

DI-0301 now has a real, worked finding on both threads: Lakeshore's nightly snapshot does genuine,
useful disaster-recovery work but isn't the 211.68(b) backup it's been informally called, and the
donor-record retention clock is a real, open policy question flagged for document control to
resolve rather than guessed at here. Next, `multi-site-governance-and-donor-identification` — this
course's final module — picks up 606.160(e)'s cumulative deferred-donor record directly, and asks
what happens when Fairview, Brookfield, and Lakeshore's central system all need to agree, in close
to real time, about the same donor's eligibility.
